extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics majors and mathematics instructors/mathematics education researchers
extracted.subtask_short: proof reading strategies for math proofs
extracted.subtask_description: Strategies and criteria for reading and comprehending undergraduate-level mathematical proofs; includes qualitative episodes of students using strategies and a survey of professors about desirability of those strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the theorem by rephrasing in one’s own words
rubrics_metrics.description: Before reading a proof, try to describe or rephrase the theorem in one’s own words to gain understanding of what is being asserted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Participants would invest time in understanding the theorem statement prior to reading its proof by reformulating it informally; this can indicate what might be assumed and what should be proven (example: Kevin reformulating Theorem 3 to see assumptions/conclusion). Survey item: instructors preferred students try to describe the theorem in their own words before reading the proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the theorem by expressing it in logical notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Express the theorem in precise logical or symbolic form (e.g., first-order notation) to clarify exactly what must be proved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Episode: Caleb and Derek co-construct ∃x ∈ R such that x^4 = x + 1 to permit algebraic reasoning. Survey item: instructors were asked whether they preferred students express the theorem in logical notation before reading its proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Try to prove the theorem before reading its proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempt to produce a proof or partial proof of the theorem yourself prior to reading the given proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benefits: makes reading active, reveals likely ‘tricks’ and techniques to be learned, makes high-level goals of the published proof transparent (example: Tim & Kevin trying to bound 4x^3 - x^4 and 2 sin x for Theorem 1). Use attempt to identify main sub-parts and expected structure; survey item asks whether instructors prefer students to try proving before reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the proof framework being used
rubrics_metrics.description: Attend explicitly to what is assumed and what is being concluded and identify the proof technique/framework (e.g., direct proof, proof by contradiction, contrapositive).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Participants noted what claim or sub-claim was being proven, the proof technique used, and how assumptions and conclusions fit within that framework; example: Kevin and Tim identifying a proof-by-contradiction sub-proof and a direct sub-proof within the same proof. This helps make invisible structural aspects visible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break or partition the proof into parts or sub-proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: For long or compound proofs, partition the proof into independent parts or sub-proofs and attend separately to each part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use partitioning to focus on high-level structure first (e.g., identify lemma and its application) and avoid becoming mired in technical details; participants sometimes skipped lemma to see main argument flow. Benefit: makes complicated proofs manageable and supports holistic understanding. Survey item: instructors asked if they preferred students break long proofs into parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check confusing inferences with examples
rubrics_metrics.description: When a step or inference is confusing, instantiate the step with a specific numerical or concrete example to see why the inference holds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example use: Caleb and Derek used n=24 to instantiate algebraic/formula steps to see how line 4 followed from line 3 in Proof 3; note distinction between mere empirical verification and using an example to reveal why a step is true. Survey item: instructors asked whether students should sometimes check assertions with numerical examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare the method used in the proof with one’s own approach
rubrics_metrics.description: After or while reading, compare the published method to the approach you would have used; reflect on differences to learn new techniques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Participants remarked when the published method differed from how they would have proceeded; benefits include identifying reusable techniques and seeing alternative problem-solving strategies. Survey item: instructors asked whether students should compare methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local understanding — know meanings of terms and the claim
rubrics_metrics.description: At a local level, understand the meaning of the terms and statements within the proof, including precisely what the claim asserts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the Mejia-Ramos et al. (2012) model: comprehension includes knowing the meaning of the theorem statement and terms; the paper documents students often fail to understand the theorem before reading the proof, so ensuring this is a component of proof comprehension assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local understanding — justify how new assertions follow
rubrics_metrics.description: Be able to justify how new assertions in the proof follow from previous ones (line-by-line logical justification).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A facet of proof comprehension: students should be able to explain the reasoning linking successive statements; empirical literature shows novices often neglect such justifications, focusing only on calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local understanding — identify the proof framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize which proof scheme/framework (e.g., direct, contradiction, contrapositive, induction) is being used and how assumptions/conclusions fit it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identification of framework helps interpret the role of assumptions and where sub-proofs begin/end; overlaps with strategy 3 but here is presented as a component of comprehension in the Mejia-Ramos model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holistic understanding — summarize high-level goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a summary of the proof that emphasizes its high-level goals and overall method rather than only line-by-line detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A holistic facet: being able to produce a concise description of what the proof achieves and the main ideas; attempts to prove beforehand and partitioning assist in producing such summaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holistic understanding — apply proof methods to new situations
rubrics_metrics.description: Be able to apply the methods or techniques used in the proof to prove new theorems or in different contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This facet emphasizes transfer: reading a proof should yield reusable insights and techniques (authors cite mathematicians’ desire that proofs teach methods). Trying to prove beforehand and comparing methods supports this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holistic understanding — break proof into main parts or sub-proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Conceptualize the proof at a macroscopic level by identifying its main parts or sub-proofs and their roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mirrors Strategy 4 and is listed as a holistic facet in the Mejia-Ramos model: useful for summarizing and for applying methods elsewhere; participants partitioned proofs to reveal subproof boundaries that linear presentation had masked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holistic understanding — apply general method to a specific example
rubrics_metrics.description: Be able to take the general ideas of a proof and show how they apply to a concrete example to illustrate mechanism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Related to Strategy 5: instantiate the general proof method on an example (not merely verify) to see why the argument works in a particular case; helps reveal invisible structure and promotes transfer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make key ideas of proofs transparent (use structured/alternative formats)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use structured proofs or alternative representations to make summary, motivation, and high-level ideas explicit and visible to readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper discusses proposals (e.g., Leron’s structured proofs) to increase transparency, noting mixed empirical evidence; authors argue engaging students productively (e.g., self-explanation) may be more effective than mere reformatting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Productive engagement / self-explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage students to actively engage with proofs (e.g., self-explanation training) so they can perceive important but initially invisible aspects of proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Hodds, Alcock, & Inglis (2014): self-explanation training produced measurable comprehension gains; authors suggest productive engagement is key for students to notice high-level proof aspects that linear presentations mask.
